Swinging on the Pendulum: Shifting Views of Justice in Human Subjects Research
  • Source: Hastings Center Report, Vol. 31, No. 3 (May-June 2001)
  • Topic: Evolution of federal research ethics policy from protection to access
  • Author(s): Anna Mastroianni, Jeffrey Kahn
Overview of Justice Shift in Research Ethics
  • 1970s --> justice = protection from research harms and exploitation
  • 1990s onward --> justice = access to benefits of research participation
  • Shift occurred rapidly despite growing evidence subjects don't fully understand research
  • Tension between protection and access creates challenges for research oversight
Historical Exploitation Driving Protection Era
  • Landmark cases emerged mid-1960s to early 1970s
Willowbrook State School Hepatitis Research
  • Institutionalized children used for hepatitis vaccine experiments
  • Parents had limited choice about children's participation
Jewish Chronic Disease Hospital Cancer Research
  • Elderly nursing home residents injected with cancer cells
  • Inadequate consent procedures
Tuskegee Syphilis Study
  • Exposed to nation in 1972
  • Decades-long study without proper consent or treatment
  • Became symbol of research exploitation
Common Patterns in Exploitation Cases
  • Inadequate attempts to inform subjects about research
  • Exploitive recruitment strategies
  • Use of vulnerable populations
  • Exposure to significant risk without direct medical benefit
  • Risks borne by subjects --> benefits accrued to others
Belmont Era: Protection Framework
  • National Commission for Protection of Human Subjects established
  • Belmont Report (1978) --> identified justice as requiring fair distribution of burdens and benefits
  • Justice interpreted primarily as prevention of exploitation
Regulatory Focus Areas
  • Protection from unacceptable risk levels
  • Prevention of exploitive participation
  • Special protections for designated vulnerable groups
Vulnerable Populations Under Protection Model
Prisoners
  • Deemed vulnerable due to constrained living environment
  • National Commission found prisoners wanted research participation for:
  • Extra income
  • Access to perks and improved health care
  • Contribution to society
  • Most powerful prisoners most likely to participate, not least powerful
  • Policy required research --> direct medical benefit OR prison environment improvement
Children
  • Deemed vulnerable due to consent reliance and exploitation potential
  • Willowbrook case highlighted vulnerability of institutionalized children
  • Regulations limited participation to:
  • Minimal risk studies, OR
  • Studies with direct medical benefit
Pregnant Women and Fetuses
  • Deemed especially vulnerable
  • Influenced by abortion debate and thalidomide memories
  • Protection expanded in practice to women of childbearing capacity
  • Policy aimed at protecting woman AND fetus from research harm
Shift to Access Emphasis (Late 1980s–1990s)
Drivers of Change
  • Growing belief research offered real benefits to participants
  • Advocacy groups argued for inclusion rights
Key Advocacy Movements
HIV/AIDS Community Leadership
  • ACT UP organized rallies during AZT trials
  • Protest signs read: "Clinical trials are health care too!"
  • Conflated research participation with medical care
  • Marked total reversal of protection-to-access ethics
Women's Health Advocacy
  • Argued exclusion policies prevented benefit access
  • Pushed for inclusion mandates
Evidence of Benefits Focus Shift
  • Best therapeutic outcomes thought to be in research protocols
  • Major investments in biomedical research yielding real applications
  • Benefits limited to populations represented in subject pools
The Exclusion Problem
  • Women excluded from research (e.g., Physicians Health Study)
  • Racial/ethnic minorities excluded
  • Children excluded from drug trials
  • Policy rationale: protection from harm and exploitation
  • Result: climate that "protected some groups to death"
  • Exclusion denies access at two levels:
  • Individual direct medical benefit
  • Group representation and generalizability
Policy Implementation: Inclusion Mandates
1994 NIH Guidelines on Women and Minorities
  • First federal policy requiring inclusion of specific groups
  • Unprecedented shift from exclusion to inclusion presumption
  • Researchers must justify any exclusion
1998 NIH Policy on Children
  • Reversed presumption about child participation
  • Special justification now required to exclude children
  • Follows similar logic to women/minority inclusion
Children and Drug Safety Problem
  • Prior policy excluded children from phase I drug trials
  • Phase I --> assess safety via escalating doses until toxicity threshold
  • Result: limited pediatric safety information
  • Children received drugs based on:
  • General size calculations relative to approved adult doses
  • Clinical experience ("trial and error")
Access Policy Examples
Arizona Cancer Clinical Trials Law (2000)
  • Required insurers to cover cancer clinical trial costs
  • Modeled on Georgia, Maryland, Rhode Island legislation
Underlying Hypothesis
  • Patients don't enroll because they must pay out-of-pocket
  • Most managed care insurers explicitly refuse experimental coverage
Problems with the Law
Enrollment Data Contradicts Hypothesis
  • Only 3% of cancer patients enroll in trials
  • Up to 20% may be eligible
  • GAO study found many factors affect enrollment beyond insurance:
  • Physician ignorance about trials
  • Physician time constraints
  • Patient reluctance to be randomized
  • Eligibility restrictions
Limited Coverage Scope
  • 24% of Arizonans uninsured (excluded)
  • Over 60% of employer-provided insurance exempt from state mandates
  • Medicare, Medicaid, VA plans not covered
Cost Impact Concerns
  • Mandate assigns costs without additional funds
  • Predictable outcomes:
  • ↑ premiums for private insurers
  • ↓ people or services covered by public programs
  • When premiums increase --> fewer people purchase insurance
Legislative Process Failures
  • Insurers' objections disregarded during drafting
  • Phase I through IV coverage mandated despite opposition
  • Insurers may "game the system" to comply with letter but not intent
Alternative Model: New Jersey Voluntary Agreement
  • Coalition covering 98% of insured NJ population agreed to pay patient care costs for trials
  • Voluntary negotiation instead of mandate
  • Demonstrates working with insurers is possible
Waiver of Informed Consent in Emergency Research (1996)
  • Federal regulations allow waiver under specific conditions
  • Represents ultimate endorsement of benefits emphasis
  • Suggests research participation so beneficial --> must guarantee access even for those unable to consent
Significance
  • Backing away from cornerstone concept of informed consent
  • Informed consent dates to Nuremberg era
  • Protection principle compromised for access
Current Era: Balancing Protection and Access
Conflicting Messages to Subjects
  • Media promotes need for research AND reports of serious harms
  • Creates confusing environment for potential subjects
High-Profile Cases Raising Concerns
Jesse Gelsinger Gene Transfer Case
  • Death in gene transfer study at University of Pennsylvania
  • Resulted in:
  • Swirl of reportage and congressional hearings
  • University investigations
  • New restrictions on gene transfer research
Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center Cases
  • Alleged conflicts of interest and failures to obtain informed consent
  • Some subjects died unexpectedly
FDA Drug Approval Concerns
  • "Seven deadly drugs" fast-tracked then withdrawn after serious side effects discovered
  • Some led to patient deaths
Current Policy Directions
  • HHS Office of Human Research Protections focusing on conflicts of interest
  • Goal: securing public trust by ensuring investigators aren't motivated to overlook protection
  • Institute of Medicine recommended IRB accreditation
Critique of Current Approaches
  • Certification and oversight focus on paperwork requirements
  • Weak proxy for adequate subject protection
  • May encourage overlooking fundamental shortcomings in research protections
Implications for Research Oversight
Protection Concerns Persist
  • Even in protection-focused era --> serious informed consent shortcomings documented
  • Subjects persistently confused about research vs. clinical care distinction
  • "Therapeutic misconception" common --> subjects overestimate personal benefit
Access Emphasis Risks
  • Overemphasis on benefits can undermine understanding of:
  • Research inherently carries risk
  • Many trials offer no direct benefit to subjects
Accountability Framework Needed
  • Balance falls to:
  • Referring physicians
  • Investigators
  • IRBs
  • Institutions
Trust as Foundation
  • Research is privilege --> not to be presumed or exploited
  • Must earn through building and maintaining public trust
  • Without public trust --> no research subjects willing to participate
  • No willingness to support research with tax dollars
Looking Ahead: Recommendations and Future Direction
Pendulum Position Assessment
  • Current climate may have swung as far toward benefits emphasis as possible
  • When pendulum finishes swing in one direction --> inevitably starts back
Signs of Return to Protection?
  • Recent HHS announcements on conflicts of interest
  • Increased regulatory oversight emphasis
  • Additional FDA funding requests (~$36 million)
Remaining Challenges
  • Paperwork requirements alone insufficient
  • May distract from efforts that properly modulate the swing
  • How far will pendulum go?
  • Do we have tools to control it?
Path Forward
  • Careful balancing of access and protection required
  • Both elements essential to ethical research enterprise
  • Public trust depends on maintaining this balance
